p: Most visitors make a beeline for the Palm House and the Temperate House, but Kew rewards those who wander off the main paths. The Princess of Wales Conservatory is a modern glasshouse with ten different climate zones under one roof, from deserts full of cacti to steamy rooms of carnivorous plants and giant waterlilies. Kids find it endlessly fascinating.

Look out for The Hive, a huge metal sculpture that hums and glows in response to the activity of real bees, and the Marianne North Gallery, a Victorian gallery lined floor to ceiling with paintings of plants from her travels around the world. Little ones should head for the Children's Garden, a big play space where they can climb, dig and explore. Kew Palace, the smallest of the royal palaces, is open seasonally and offers a glimpse into Georgian royal life.

Seasons change everything here. Spring brings carpets of bluebells and blossom, summer is all about long days on the lawns, autumn turns the trees into a riot of reds and golds, and in winter the Christmas at Kew light trail draws big crowds after dark. Book ahead for that one.

Picnics are welcome on the lawns, so pack a lunch and grab a shady spot. Allow most of a day if you can, and don't forget that the Thames Path runs alongside, so a riverside stroll towards Richmond is an easy way to finish off.
